framework.name: Common Core State Standards
framework.source: https://corestandards.org (English Language Arts and Mathematics; objective wording is the school's own)

objectives.description: Support an analysis of a short story by citing the strongest evidence from the text, and say what the text leaves unstated.
Explain how a complex character's choices and motives move a plot forward and shape the theme.
Interpret figurative and connotative language in a literary passage, including how specific word choices set tone.
Trace a theme through a story and describe how the author shapes and refines it over the course of the text.
Analyze how an author's decisions about order, pacing and time create suspense, surprise or tension.
Compare how a work from another culture and a US work approach a shared idea, with attention to point of view.
Recognize how an author draws on a myth or classic story, and explain what the later work does with it.
Select textual evidence that most strongly supports a claim about a nonfiction text.
Determine the central idea of an informational text and summarize how it builds across paragraphs.
Analyze how an author introduces, links and develops a series of ideas or events.
Identify an author's purpose and point of view and explain the rhetoric used to advance it.
Write a narrative with a clear point of view, pacing, sensory detail and a reflective ending.
Write an informative essay that organizes ideas under a clear thesis with relevant facts and examples.
Write an argument that states a precise claim, supports it with reasons and evidence, and addresses a counterclaim.
Plan, revise and edit writing after feedback, and say what each revision changed.
Contribute to a seminar discussion by preparing in advance, building on others' points and keeping to agreed rules.
Use phrases and clauses to add variety and precision to sentences.
Work out the meaning of unfamiliar words from context, word parts and reference tools.
Cite the strongest textual evidence for an interpretation of a longer literary work, and mark where the text is ambiguous.
Follow a theme across a novel or play and explain how it is developed through characters and events.
Analyze how complex characters relate to one another and to the larger conflict.
Analyze the effect of repeated words, images and symbols on meaning and mood.
Explain how the structure of a play or novel, including its acts, chapters or turning points, shapes its effect.
Compare a written scene with a staged or filmed version and explain what each interpretation emphasizes.
Read and comprehend a range of grade-level literature, independently and with growing stamina.
Analyze how an author's word choices in a speech or essay shape its tone and meaning.
Analyze how an author structures an argument and how the parts connect to the whole.
Evaluate an argument, separating valid reasoning from unsupported or fallacious claims.
Compare how two foundational US documents or speeches address a similar concept.
Write a literary argument with a precise claim, organized reasons, evidence and a counterclaim.
Write an explanatory essay that develops a topic with well-chosen facts, quotations and transitions.
Carry out a short research project, narrowing the question as the sources suggest.
Gather relevant information from several sources, assess their credibility and cite them without plagiarizing.
Draw evidence from literary and informational texts to support analysis in writing.
Present findings clearly and logically so that listeners can follow the line of reasoning.
Use a colon or semicolon correctly, and spell and punctuate with care in finished work.
Cite strong evidence for what a text says directly and what it implies, and weigh where it is uncertain.
Determine two or more themes in a work of American literature and analyze how they interact.
Analyze how an author's choices about setting, character and plot create effects such as irony or ambiguity.
Analyze how language that is rich or ambiguous contributes to meaning and tone across a text.
Analyze a point of view in which what is directly stated differs from what is meant, such as satire or understatement.
Show how foundational works of American literature treat similar themes across different periods.
Evaluate evidence that supports inferences drawn from an essay or speech.
Evaluate the effectiveness of the structure an author uses to make a point engaging or persuasive.
Evaluate an author's reasoning and rhetoric in a seminal US text, including the appeals used.
Delineate and evaluate the reasoning in a Supreme Court opinion or other public document.
Write an argument that sets out a claim, distinguishes it from alternatives and supports it with valid reasoning.
Write an informative essay that organizes complex ideas and sustains a formal style.
Write a narrative that uses technique such as dialogue, reflection and shifting pace to convey experience.
Conduct a sustained research project, synthesizing several sources on a focused question.
Draw evidence from literary or informational texts, including a work of American literature, to support analysis.
Lead and take part in discussions that respond to a range of perspectives and move toward a decision.
Present information so that organization, development and style suit the audience and task.
Vary syntax for effect, consulting style guides when writing for a particular audience.
Support a reading of a British or world work with precise evidence, and show how the text complicates a first impression.
Trace the development of two or more themes in a work and show how they connect.
Analyze how a character's choices in a drama or novel are shaped by the setting and the conflict.
Analyze how an author's choices about structure and timing shape the meaning and aesthetic effect of a work.
Evaluate multiple interpretations of a story, play or poem, drawing on specific passages.
Read and comprehend literature at the high end of the grades 11 to 12 range.
Determine the central ideas of a complex text and provide an objective summary.
Analyze how a writer's treatment of an event or idea changes as the text moves forward.
Integrate and evaluate information from several sources presented in different media.
Analyze documents of historical and literary significance for their themes, purposes and rhetoric.
Write a sustained argument on a question of public concern, with a precise claim and counterclaims answered.
Write a personal essay or explanatory text with a controlling idea and a polished, formal style.
Revise for focus, organization and style, drawing on peer and teacher feedback.
Gather and assess information from several authoritative print and digital sources and cite them in a standard format.
Integrate multiple sources of information, evaluating their credibility, when preparing a presentation.
Evaluate a speaker's point of view, reasoning and use of evidence and rhetoric.
Interpret figures of speech and subtle shades of word meaning in context.
Acquire and use academic and domain-specific vocabulary accurately for college and career readiness.
Evaluate how a news writer's word choice and framing reveal a point of view.
Compare how the same event is reported in print, broadcast and online sources.
Tell reporting that supports its claims with evidence from opinion or advertising dressed as news.
Write a news story in inverted-pyramid form that answers who, what, where, when, why and how.
Write a feature story that opens with a scene and organizes information around a central idea.
Write an editorial that takes a clear position and answers the strongest objection.
Write headlines, ledes and captions that are accurate, concise and suited to the audience.
Use digital tools to produce, publish and update a school news page.
Plan a reporting project from a focused question to a published piece.
Gather information from interviews and documents, check facts and attribute sources properly.
Conduct an interview with prepared questions and follow-ups, and report the answers fairly.
Present a short broadcast or podcast segment with a clear structure and a steady delivery.
Apply Associated Press style conventions for numbers, titles and attribution.
Edit copy for grammar, spelling and punctuation to a publishable standard.
Choose precise, plain language over jargon when writing for a general audience.
Explain how the First Amendment and school press rulings bear on what a student newspaper may print.
Choose units that suit a real situation and use them to interpret formulas and graphs.
Interpret the parts of an expression, such as terms, factors and coefficients, in context.
Write and solve linear equations in one variable from a word problem.

strands.strand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities

objectives.description: Explain each step in solving an equation as following from the equality of the previous step.
Solve linear equations and inequalities in one variable, including those with letter coefficients.
Rearrange a formula to isolate a quantity of interest.
Represent constraints with equations or inequalities and interpret solutions as viable or not.
Explain what makes a relation a function and use function notation to describe it.
Evaluate functions for inputs in their domains and interpret the results in context.
Read a graph or table of a function to describe where it rises, falls, and reaches intercepts.
Calculate and interpret the average rate of change of a function over an interval.
Graph linear functions and show intercepts.
Write equations in two variables to represent a relationship and graph them on axes.
Write a linear function that describes a relationship between two quantities.

strands.strand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities

objectives.description: Explain that the graph of an equation in two variables is the set of all its solutions.
Solve a system of two linear equations by graphing and substitution.
Solve a system of two linear equations by elimination, and explain why it works.
Graph a linear inequality in two variables and a system of them.
State precise definitions of angle, circle, perpendicular line, parallel line and line segment.

strands.strand: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations
strands.subStrand: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations

objectives.description: Use coordinates to find distances and the perimeter of polygons.
Represent transformations in the plane and describe them as functions on points.
Draw the image of a figure under a rotation, reflection or translation, and describe the sequence that maps one figure to another.
Use rigid motions to decide whether two figures are congruent.
Use the definition of congruence in terms of rigid motions to show that two triangles are congruent.
Explain how the SSS, SAS and ASA criteria follow from the definition of congruence.
Prove theorems about lines and angles, such as vertical angles and angles formed by a transversal.

strands.strand: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations
strands.subStrand: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations

objectives.description: Prove the slope criteria for parallel and perpendicular lines and use them to solve problems.
Make formal constructions with a compass and straightedge and explain why they work.
Prove theorems about triangles, including the angle sum and the midsegment theorem.
Prove theorems about isosceles triangles and the points of concurrency of a triangle.
Prove theorems about parallelograms and use them to classify quadrilaterals.

strands.strand: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations
strands.subStrand: Geometry: Expressing Geometric Properties with Equations

objectives.description: Use coordinates to prove simple geometric theorems algebraically.

strands.strand: Geometry: Similarity, Right Triangles and Trigonometry
strands.subStrand: Geometry: Similarity, Right Triangles and Trigonometry

objectives.description: Verify the effects of a dilation on lines and segments.
Use similarity transformations to decide whether two figures are similar.
Use similarity to establish the AA criterion for two triangles.
Use congruence and similarity criteria to solve problems and prove relationships in figures.
Graph and compare the parent functions: linear, quadratic, absolute value, square root and cube root.
Describe how a graph changes when a function is shifted, stretched or reflected.
Combine functions by arithmetic and composition to model a situation.
Find the inverse of a function and verify it by composition.

strands.strand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities

objectives.description: Solve absolute-value, radical and rational equations in one variable and identify extraneous solutions.
Write and solve inequalities and compound inequalities from a context.
Recognize the structure of an expression and rewrite it, such as a difference of squares.

strands.strand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities

objectives.description: Solve quadratic equations by factoring, completing the square and the quadratic formula.
Choose the form of a quadratic that reveals its zeros, vertex or axis of symmetry.

strands.strand: Number and Quantity: The Complex Number System
strands.subStrand: Number and Quantity: The Complex Number System

objectives.description: Write and compute with complex numbers of the form a plus bi.
Solve quadratic equations with real coefficients that have complex solutions.

strands.strand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities

objectives.description: Solve a system of a linear equation and a quadratic equation in two variables.

strands.strand: Algebra: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

objectives.description: Add, subtract and multiply polynomials and recognize that they are closed under those operations.
Apply the remainder theorem to test whether a number is a root of a polynomial.
Find the zeros of a polynomial from a factored form and use them to sketch its graph.
Prove polynomial identities and use them to describe numerical relationships.
Graph polynomial functions, showing zeros, end behavior and turning points.
Represent constraints with equations and inequalities and interpret a solution as viable or not.
Describe the key features of a function: domain, range, intercepts, intervals of increase, extrema and end behavior.
Describe how transformations change the graph and equation of a function.
Combine functions by arithmetic and composition, and find the domain of the result.
Find and restrict the domain of an inverse function.
Graph polynomial functions, showing zeros, multiplicity and end behavior.

strands.strand: Algebra: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

objectives.description: Use the remainder and factor theorems to factor polynomials and find rational zeros.

strands.strand: Number and Quantity: The Complex Number System
strands.subStrand: Number and Quantity: The Complex Number System

objectives.description: Use the fundamental theorem of algebra to count the zeros of a polynomial.

strands.strand: Algebra: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Arithmetic with Polynomials and Rational Expressions

objectives.description: Rewrite rational expressions by long division or by factoring.
Graph rational functions and find vertical, horizontal and slant asymptotes.

strands.strand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities
strands.subStrand: Algebra: Reasoning with Equations and Inequalities

objectives.description: Solve rational and radical equations and rational inequalities.

strands.strand: Functions: Linear, Quadratic and Exponential Models
strands.subStrand: Functions: Linear, Quadratic and Exponential Models

objectives.description: Model growth and decay with exponential functions and solve with logarithms.
Graph logarithmic functions and relate them to exponentials as inverses.

strands.strand: Functions: Linear, Quadratic and Exponential Models
strands.subStrand: Functions: Linear, Quadratic and Exponential Models

objectives.description: Use the properties of logarithms to solve exponential and logarithmic equations.
Define radian measure and relate it to arc length on the unit circle.
Extend the trigonometric functions to all real numbers using the unit circle.
Model periodic phenomena with trigonometric functions and choose amplitude, period and midline.
Describe the end behavior and asymptotes of a function using limit notation informally.
Find an average rate of change over an interval and interpret it as the slope of a secant line.
